newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan-Fed should not fine-tune US labor market.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan-Fed should not fine-tune US labor market.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve will be watching developments with wages to gauge whether inflation may be set to increase, but policymakers are not interested in "fine-tuning" the labor market, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said Tuesday.

Greenspan, who was responding to a question during an appearance before the Senate Budget Committee, described U.S. labor markets as "exceptionally tight" but said that so far that has not led to accelerated wages and higher inflation.
Because of that, the Fed has chosen not to raise interest rates in response to the labor market developments, he said.

However, Greenspan cautioned, "Should it become evident that indeed the process of inflation is beginning to emerge -- granted that our policies become effective with a lag -- then we have to focus on the process of inflation."
To the extent that tight labor markets could become a part of that process, Greenspan said the Fed will look carefully at that sector.
Still, he added, "The last thing we want to do is to inhibit economic growth to try to fine-tune the various different aspects of labor markets or other areas."
The Fed chief was also questioned about his estimate of a a perceived upward bias in the Consumer Price Index.
He said the Fed's research pointed to a bias of around 1.0 percentage point a year or a range of around 0.6 point to 1.5 points.
A congressionally appointed panel led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin pegged the CPI overstatement at around 1.1 percentage point a year.
Greenspan also said that he thought widespread investment by consumers in mutual funds was a good thing, saying it was a "plus."
He told the committee that, in the past, individual investors invested in individual stocks but that it was less risky for them to put their funds into mutual funds.
